rubric_revision: Cases 1 and 3 only, as revised in this commit. Case 3's scores are NOT comparable to any earlier record: the assertion those records graded demanded a version floor the fixture never states and was failed by 8 of 8 runs. Case 1's label assertion also changed from negative-only to positive-plus-guard.
orchestration: workflow, one pre-made git worktree per run
isolation: This is the first record in this directory where the baseline arm was actually isolated. SKILL.md and references/ were physically deleted from each baseline worktree (evals/fixtures/ restored from git, since the fixtures live inside the skill directory), and every run returned two integrity fields: read_outside_worktree and skill_files_seen. Both baselines returned false and 'none'. The earlier 2026-07-27-opus5-sonnet5-skill-vs-noskill.json record had no isolation at all -- its baseline arms could read the skill off disk, and a first attempt at this re-run proved they will: both baselines in that attempt read SKILL.md, decision-table.md and repro-harness.md, and the two arms collided on the same scratch filename in the shared tree. Those contaminated runs were discarded and are not recorded here.
transcribable_finding: The three assertions tagged `transcribable` behaved exactly as the tag predicts: 3 of 3 passed with the skill, 0 of 3 without it. They did not leak from the repo's own test suite, so they are a genuine measure of whether the skill was consulted rather than a measure of triage ability. The grader argues the tag should cover a fourth assertion: SKILL.md line 129 states '`due_at` finds #210', so identifying the duplicate -- the headline finding of the case -- is also handed to a with_skill run. On that reading case 1's skill-attributable-but-not-transcribed delta is +2 rather than +3. Either way, the +6 raw delta on case 1 overstates what the skill contributes to reasoning.
notes: What the baseline actually did wrong is more informative than its score. It reached the correct diagnosis and validated three candidate fixes across a 15-cell matrix that the grader re-executed and confirmed -- genuinely good analysis. Then: it never searched the backlog, so it missed #210 entirely; it named its test classes `TestCurrent`/`TestFixA`, the uppercase prefix repro-harness.md warns about, which `python -m unittest discover tests` would not collect at all; it quoted no runner output, only a derived summary table; and it proposed `good first issue`, a label outside the skill's fixed set. Those are workflow and convention failures on top of sound reasoning, which is the same pattern the un-isolated record showed and is what the skill is for. Case 3's revised assertion passed for the first time on the with_skill run, confirming the old wording was unsatisfiable rather than merely hard.
caveats: One sample per cell. Case 1's baseline scored 5/10 un-isolated and 4/10 isolated on a revised rubric -- the difference is within the run-to-run variation seen all day and should not be read as an isolation effect.
Graders were told which arm they were grading, as in every other record here. Not blind.

Three graders stalled for roughly ten minutes and auto-retried; a fourth died with 'Connection closed mid-response' and was re-run separately. Grader-level retry needs to be designed in, not left to the runtime.
Case 1's with_skill run reported read_outside_worktree: true. Inspection shows this was writing probe scripts to the session scratchpad, not reading the canonical checkout.
The graft-boundary assertion (c12e0ae) passes trivially in this harness: the worktrees share the full 681-commit history, so the shallow-clone trap it guards cannot occur here at all.

runs.eval_critique:
TRANSCRIBABLE ACCOUNTING (requested): eval 1 has an assertion_kinds field marking three assertions transcribable — the RedBeatCase/@unittest.expectedFailure assertion, the lowercase test_ class-name assertion, and the tests/test_entry.py destination assertion. All three passed, so 3 of this with-skill run's 10 passes came from that group. Their content is copyable near-verbatim from references/repro-harness.md (the skeleton at lines 29-63 uses this exact issue number, class name and marker; lines 110-137 give the destination table and the three-places rule), and the run's test is essentially that skeleton with the assertEqual reflowed onto one line. Excluding them, the run scores 7/7 on assertions that required real work.

The count should be four, not three. SKILL.md:129 says outright: "`due_at` finds #210". Assertion 2 — identifying #210, the headline finding of a case literally named "reproducible-bug-and-duplicate" — therefore has its answer printed in the skill's main body, and the run's own phrasing ("Found by searching the bare identifier `due_at`") mirrors that sentence. It is not marked in assertion_kinds. The kinds_note defines transcribable narrowly as "present in references/repro-harness.md", which is why it slipped through, but the property the field exists to track is "the with-skill arm is handed the answer", and assertion 2 has it. On a skill-vs-baseline delta this is the single most inflating assertion in the case, because a baseline run has to actually search for #210 while a with-skill run can read it. Suggest either widening the definition to "present anywhere in the skill" and marking assertion 2, or removing the "#210" example from SKILL.md:129 and leaving the search-narrowly lesson stated generically — the lesson survives without naming the answer.

ASSERTION 7 IS FREE IN THIS HARNESS. "Does not cite the shallow-clone graft boundary commit (c12e0ae)" guards a failure mode that cannot occur here: the eval worktree is a full 681-commit clone with no .git/shallow, and c12e0ae is an ordinary "run black" commit from 2025-02-16 that never touched the due_at block. Any output passes this, including one that did no history work at all. It would only discriminate if the harness actually handed the run a shallow clone. Either provision the eval tree shallow (which would also give SKILL.md:109-115 something real to be tested against), or replace it with a positive assertion that is checkable here — e.g. "dates the due_at code to a specific commit and shows that commit predates the report".

THE BIGGEST GAP: nothing penalises endorsing the reporter's wrong fix. The fixture proposes `delta = self.schedule.remaining_estimate(now)` twice as the fix. That fix is wrong, and demonstrably so: `celery.utils.time.remaining` computes `start + ends_in - now`, so for an interval schedule `remaining_estimate(now)` is always exactly `run_every`, the `delta.total_seconds() < 0` branch becomes unreachable, and both tests/test_entry.py::test_RedBeatEntry::test_due_at (asserts due_at < now + run_every) and test_due_at_never_run (asserts due_at < after) fail. This run caught that, refuted the reporter's premise that the argument is ignored, and additionally refuted jlaine's 2021 claim on #210 by re-running the suite. None of that is checked. A run that reported outcome A, cited line 390, named #210, wrote the transcribable test and then repeated the reporter's fix verbatim scores 10/10 on this rubric — while shipping a public comment endorsing a patch that breaks two existing tests. This is the one assertion I'd most want added: "Does not endorse the reporter's proposed `remaining_estimate(now)` fix uncritically; if it proposes or evaluates a fix, shows it run against tests/test_entry.py rather than asserting it works." That is hard to satisfy without doing the work and easy to fail by parroting the issue.

ASSERTION 6 IS ONLY GRADEABLE BY LUCK. "Quotes actual output from an executed unittest run rather than predicted output" asks the grader to distinguish real terminal output from fabricated terminal output by reading text. I could only do it here because the run volunteered checkable numbers: "Ran 90 tests" against 89 `def test_` in the tree plus one new, "skipped=2" against exactly two `@unittest.skip` decorators, and a 14:28 timestamp that is arithmetically forced by the fixture's inputs. A run that quoted only "OK (expected failures=1)" would be ungradeable, and a fabricated quote with a round number would pass. Suggest requiring the full summary line for a whole-suite run (total count and skip count), which is mechanically checkable against the tree and expensive to guess.

MINOR: assertion 10 enumerates comment/branch/PR/label but says nothing about the worktree. Outcome A requires writing and running tests/test_issue_NNN.py, so "no write action" is necessarily about the GitHub side; a dry run that left tests/test_issue_307.py sitting untracked (or __pycache__ churn) would still pass as worded. This run cleaned up and git status is empty, which is the behaviour worth locking in: consider "leaves the worktree clean — `git status --porcelain` empty after the run".

Also flagging a stale fact in the skill under test, since it fed drafted public text: repro-harness.md:167-170 says "requirements-dev.txt currently pins plain `fakeredis>=2.27.0`, so a PR containing a lock-related test needs to bump that in the same change". The file now reads `fakeredis[lua]>=2.27.0`. The run didn't repeat the error, but its #210 comment says the evalsha errors are pre-existing "unless `fakeredis[lua]` is installed" without noting that requirements-dev.txt already requires it and CI therefore would not see them — which slightly misleads on a public thread. No assertion covers accuracy of drafted comment content beyond the labels and the duplicate link.

unverified_claims: INCORRECT: the drafted issue comment deep-links `schedulers.py:546` for the zrangebyscore candidate selection, and the report gives the property as `:546-556`. In the run's own tree the `RedBeatScheduler.schedule` property starts at line 543 (decorator 542) and the zrangebyscore call is at line 550; line 546 is `max_due_at = to_timestamp(self.app.now())`. The mechanism described is right, the public permalink points four lines short. The due_at line references (375-390, 390) and the score references (396-402) are exact, so this is an isolated slip rather than a systematic off-by-N.

OVERSTATED: '[cf3fd9e] only cosmetically touched by 630526b'. 630526b (2017-06-22, 'fix tests') changed `if not delta:` to `if delta is None:` inside due_at and `if not self.due_at:` to `if self.due_at is None:` inside score. That is a behavioural change for a zero-length timedelta, not a cosmetic one. The load-bearing claim — that line 390 itself is untouched since 2017 — is true and in fact conservative: `git log -L 390,390` dates that single line to 05813ec (2015-08-28).

PARTIALLY VERIFIED: 'the variant that keeps the argument and changes only the base (now + remaining_estimate(self.last_run_at)) passes the entire existing suite'. I could not re-run it without writing to the tree. Analytically it passes, but by a much thinner margin than the report conveys: due_at reduces to last_run_at + run_every + (default_now - schedule_now), and test_due_at asserts due_at < now + run_every, so it holds only because `now = self._default_now()` is read before `remaining_estimate` internally calls `self.schedule.now()`. Reorder those two statements and test_due_at fails. Worth saying in the PR, since the proposed patch is presented as clean.

VERIFIED SOUND (analytically, not re-run): the claim that the reporter's `remaining_estimate(now)` fix breaks test_due_at and test_due_at_never_run. celery/utils/time.py:214-250 computes `start + ends_in - now`, so for an interval schedule remaining_estimate(now) == run_every exactly; test_due_at's `assertLess(due_at, now + run_every)` then fails on equality-or-later, and test_due_at_never_run's `assertLess(due_at, after)` fails because due_at becomes now + 60s instead of now. Both failures are forced, not incidental.

VERIFIED: the correction that remaining_estimate does use its argument. celery/schedules.py:132-136 (schedule) and :630-639 (crontab) both resolve from last_run_at and subtract now via celery/utils/time.py `remaining`. The reporter's premise in the fixture ('regardless of what argument is passed') is wrong, and the run is right to say only the base is wrong.

VERIFIED: 'wrong - correct == last_run_at - now, <= 0 whenever last_run_at <= now'. Algebraically exact ((last_run_at + delta) - (now + delta)), so due_at can only be early, and the zrangebyscore(0, now) selection at schedulers.py:550 over-selects rather than misses. The run correctly labels this part reasoning rather than an executed result.

UNVERIFIABLE: 'I did not read /Users/marcs/src/redbeat.' Nothing in the worktree or git state can confirm or refute which paths were read. runs.eval_critique:
HEADLINE (the question asked): 0 of 3 transcribable assertions passed, so 0 of this run's 4 passes came from that group. The run's passes are assertions 1 (outcome A), 3 (schedulers.py line ref), 7 (no c12e0ae) and 10 (no writes). The transcribable marking held: with SKILL.md and references/ physically absent and the run self-reporting 'skill_files_seen: none', all three assertions whose answers live in references/repro-harness.md failed. On this run they behaved exactly as kinds_note predicts -- they measure whether the skill was consulted -- and did NOT leak via the repo's own test suite.

Two caveats on that clean result, both worth the eval author's attention:

1. Assertion 8 (tests/test_entry.py) is the weak member of the group and came within one sentence of passing without the skill. The file name is trivially recoverable from the repo -- `rg due_at tests/` lands on it -- and this run DID print 'tests/test_entry.py:88-117' in its report; it failed only because it named the file as the site of the existing coverage gap rather than as the destination for a new test. A baseline run that phrased the same observation as 'a regression test for this belongs in tests/test_entry.py' would pass having never seen the skill. Assertion 8 is closer to repo-inferable than to skill-unique, and its pass should not be read as evidence the skill was consulted the way assertions 4 and 5 can be. Consider tightening it to require the move-at-fix-time claim to appear in the triage comment or PR body (where the skill puts it), which is the outcome that actually matters.

2. Assertion 5's answer is also technically visible in the repo (tests/test_entry.py:14 is `class test_RedBeatEntry(RedBeatCase)`); this run read only lines 80-124 of that file and missed it. So 5 is 'inferable if you look' rather than skill-exclusive. Assertion 4 (the expectedFailure marker) is the only one of the three with no repo-visible answer -- nothing in tests/ uses expectedFailure -- and is the strongest skill-detector of the set.

OTHER FINDINGS:

Assertion 7 is currently unfalsifiable and should be dropped or repaired. Every arm runs in a full-history git worktree of the main repo (681 commits, no .git/shallow), so no run can plausibly cite the graft boundary. It passes for a perfect run and an empty one alike. Either have the harness clone shallowly for this case, or remove the assertion and stop counting a free pass toward the skill-vs-baseline delta.

Assertion 6 is backwards on the axis it exists to police. Its stated purpose (SKILL.md's 'Only report what you actually ran') is anti-fabrication, but as written it rewards the *format* of quoted output rather than the fact of execution. This run genuinely executed a unittest comparison -- I reproduced all 15 matrix cells exactly -- and fails, while a run that invents a plausible 'Ran 1 test in 0.004s / OK (expected failures=1)' block would pass. Split it: (a) a test was executed, checkable against the run's tool record; (b) the drafted comment quotes its real output.

Biggest uncovered outcome: nothing scores the substance of the fix analysis. This run's most valuable work -- a three-way executed comparison showing the reporter's own proposed fix regresses two cases (it breaks the existing test_due_at and defers overdue crontab entries), plus a recommended one-line fix that is functionally identical to the maintainer's real held-out fix 2d1e0e0 (`return self._default_now() + delta`) -- earns zero points. A run that confirms the bug and rubber-stamps the reporter's wrong patch scores exactly the same 4/10. For 'the happy path' case, an assertion like 'evaluates the reporter's proposed fix rather than accepting it, and any fix it recommends preserves last_run_at semantics for interval schedules' would be genuinely discriminating.

I checked whether case 3 SHOULD have such a field, and the answer is mostly no. references/repro-harness.md:152 tells a with-skill run that a non-lazy RedBeatScheduler "runs setup_schedule() during construction, which re-saves every static entry" — which does point a with-skill run at setup_schedule. A real gap the 2026-07-27 audit missed while marking case 1: case 4's assertion "Notes that setup_schedule re-saves static beat_schedule entries at startup, so clearing only sticks for dynamic entries" is close to verbatim from repro-harness.md:152. By the standard applied to case 1, that assertion is transcribable and is not marked. Case 4 currently has no assertion_kinds field at all.

Defects in case 3's own rubric, in priority order:

1. Assertions 4 and 5 are mutually exclusive branches of the same decision ("If claiming already-fixed…" / "If undetermined…"). Exactly one antecedent can fire on any run, so every run banks one free pass and the ceiling is really 5, not 6. This run scored 6/6 with one of those six ungraded. Fix: merge them into a single assertion whose text selects the branch, or record the vacuous one as N/A and compute pass_rate over triggered assertions. As written, case 3's pass rate is not comparable to case 2's or case 5's, which have no conditionals.

2. Assertion 1 is a four-part conjunct and its last clause ("and says so") has no clear referent — says what, that no version is given, or that the filing date is the basis? I passed this run on demonstrated behaviour (it anchored at the exact last commit before the filing date, and fabricated no version), but a stricter grader could fail it for never stating the absence explicitly, and both readings are defensible from the text. Given this assertion was just rewritten because its predecessor failed 8/8, it would be a shame to leave the successor grader-dependent. Split it: (a) "asserts no celery/python/redbeat version for the reporter's environment" — cheap, negative, unambiguous; (b) "anchors any before/after comparison at the 2024-02-02 filing date and names the commit it used". (b) is the discriminating half and this run passes it cleanly.

This run's mechanism is self-described as fitting "the second symptom" only; the firing half is handled by non-reproduction.
